newsitem.title: CANADA: Imperial plans big Alberta heavy oil line.
newsitem.headline: Imperial plans big Alberta heavy oil line.

text.p: Imperial Oil Ltd is joining a crowded roster of Canadian energy companies in planning its own C$200 million-C$250 million pipeline to carry heavy oil from northeastern Alberta, an Imperial spokesman said on Tuesday.

Imperial, Canada's biggest energy company, has begun talking to various stakeholders about its plans to boost pipeline capacity to Hardisty, Alberta from its huge Cold Lake, Alberta bitumen project, Imperial's Hart Searle told Reuters.
"We're taking a very serious look at it," Searle said. "When we look at our other options, so far it's economically attractive."
Imperial's plans are latest in a string of proposals aimed at boosting transport capacity for Canada's growing heavy oil production.
IPL Energy Inc and Suncor Energy Inc said on Monday they would combine their Athabasca-region pipeline proposals into one C$325 million project, with a capacity of of more than 500,000 barrels a day.

The move came two weeks after Alberta Energy Co Ltd and Husky Oil Ltd announced plans for their joint Lakeland Pipeline system, a C$400 million project with an initial capacity of 150,000 barrels of heavy oil a day.
Shell Canada Ltd has also served notice it might build a pipeline to its Scotford refinery in Edmonton from its proposed oil sands project in the region.

Searle said Imperial's project, aimed at carrying growing bitumen volumes from Cold Lake -- Canada's second-largest oil source -- could be before Alberta regulators by the end of the year for proposed startup by the turn of the century.
Cold Lake output is expected to average 115,000 barrels a day this year, and phased expansion is expected to bring boost output to 150,000 by 2000 and 165,000 after 2000.

Searle said Imperial's plans included a 24-inch line to carry bitumen to Hardisty -- a key connection point with IPL's Interprovincial and start of the Express export pipelines -- from Cold Lake. The bitumen line would have an initial capacity of 100,000 barrels a day.

The system would also include a 12-inch pipeline to carry 25,000 barrels a day of diluent back to Cold Lake from Hardisty, he said. Diluent is added to bitumen to allow the thick heavy oil to flow in pipelines.
Searle said he did not know if the other operators had talked to Imperial about signing up for their projects, but suspected that was the case.

"We're certainly open to commercial negotiations with other folks who may want to join our project," he said. "But that doesn't mean our ears are closed to listening to others." ((Jeffrey Jones, Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
